{{Short description|Chaotic dynamical system, a type of "billiards"}}

In [[physics]] and [[mathematics]], the '''Hadamard dynamical system''' (also called '''Hadamard's billiard''' or the '''Hadamard–Gutzwiller model'''<ref>{{cite journal|first1=R.|last1=Aurich|first2=M.|last2=Sieber|first3=F.|last3=Steiner|title=Quantum Chaos of the Hadamard–Gutzwiller Model|journal=Physical Review Letters|date=1 August 1988|pages=483–487|volume=61|issue=5|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.61.483|pmid=10039347|bibcode=1988PhRvL..61..483A|url=http://bib-pubdb1.desy.de/record/324018/files/PhysRevLett61483.pdf}}</ref>) is a [[chaos theory|chaotic]] [[dynamical system]], a type of [[dynamical billiards]]. Introduced by [[Jacques Hadamard]] in 1898,<ref>{{cite journal|first = Jacques|last = Hadamard|year = 1898|title = Les surfaces à courbures opposées et leurs lignes géodesiques|journal = Journal de Mathématiques Pures et Appliquées|volume = 4|pages = 27–73|url=https://www.numdam.org/item/JMPA_1898_5_4__27_0.pdf}}</ref> and studied by [[Martin Gutzwiller]] in the 1980s,<ref>{{cite journal|first1=M. C.|last1=Gutzwiller|title=Classical Quantization of a Hamiltonian with Ergodic Behavior|journal=Physical Review Letters|date=21 July 1980|pages=150–153|volume=45|issue=3|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.45.150|bibcode=1980PhRvL..45..150G}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|first1=M. C.|last1=Gutzwiller|title=The Geometry of Quantum Chaos|journal=Physica Scripta|date=1985|pages=184–192|volume=T9|doi=10.1088/0031-8949/1985/T9/030|bibcode=1985PhST....9..184G}}</ref> 

The system considers the motion of a free ([[friction]]less) [[Subatomic particle|particle]] on a surface with constant negative [[curvature]]. 

==History==
It is probably the first dynamical system to be proven [[Chaos theory|chaotic]]<ref>{{cite journal|title=Chaos on the pseudosphere|first1=N.L. |last1=Balazs(Saclay)|first2=A.|last2=Voros(Saclay)|date=Jun 1986 | journal=Phys. Rep.|volume=143 |number=143|pages=109–240|doi=10.1016/0370-1573(86)90159-6 |bibcode=1986PhR...143..109B |url=https://inspirehep.net/literature/226843}}</ref>
, essentially proving that it bounces back and forward between multiple limit points in some shape of ergodic manner<ref>{{cite journal|journal=Hamburg Math.|volume=Abh. 3|year=1924| pages=170–175|first=E.|last=Artin|title=Ein mechanisches System mit quasiergodischen Bahnen.|doi=10.1007/BF02954622 |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02954622|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{cite book | title=Collected Papers|first=E.|last=Artin| publisher=Addison Wesley, New York| year=1965| pages=499–501}}</ref>
<ref>{{cite book | title=Ergodentheorie|first=E.|last=Hopf| publisher=Springer, Berlin| year=1937| pages=67|doi=10.1007/978-3-642-86630-2 |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-642-86630-2}}</ref>

Hadamard was able to show that every particle trajectory moves away from every other in an unstable and hyperbolic fashion, with a geometrical argument about the angles in between trajectories.<ref>{{cite journal|first = Jacques|last = Hadamard|year = 1898|title = Les surfaces à courbures opposées et leurs lignes géodesiques|journal = Journal de Mathématiques Pures et Appliquées|volume = 4|pages = 27–73|url=https://www.numdam.org/item/JMPA_1898_5_4__27_0.pdf}}</ref> In modern terminology this means that that the system is always unstable, what is more important is that all trajectories have a positive [[Lyapunov exponent]] and therefore chaotic behaviour. Hadamard had the intuition of chaos, but did not explicitly used the Lyapunov exponents or ergodic theory.{{citation needed|date=July 2025}}

Frank Steiner argues that Hadamard's study should be considered to be the first-ever examination of a chaotic dynamical system, and that Hadamard should be considered the first discoverer of chaos.<ref>{{Cite book |first=Frank |last=Steiner |chapter=Quantum Chaos |title=Schlaglichter der Forschung: Zum 75. Jahrestag der Universität Hamburg 1994 |editor-first=R. |editor-last=Ansorge |year=1994 |location=Berlin |publisher=Reimer |pages=542–564 |isbn=978-3-496-02540-5 |arxiv=chao-dyn/9402001 |bibcode=1994chao.dyn..2001S }}</ref> He points out that the study was widely disseminated, and considers the impact of the ideas on the thinking of [[Albert Einstein]] and [[Ernst Mach]].

The system is particularly important in that in 1963, [[Yakov Sinai]], in studying [[Sinai's billiards]] as a model of the classical ensemble of a Boltzmann–Gibbs gas, was able to show that the motion of the atoms in the gas follow the trajectories in the Hadamard dynamical system.

==Exposition==
The motion studied is that of a free particle sliding frictionlessly on the surface, namely, one having the [[Hamiltonian mechanics|Hamiltonian]]

:<math>H(p,q)=\frac{1}{2m} p_i p_j g^{ij}(q)</math>

where ''m'' is the mass of the particle, <math>q^i</math>, <math>i=1,2</math> are the coordinates on the manifold, <math>p_i</math> are the [[conjugate momenta]]:

:<math>p_i=mg_{ij} \frac{dq^j}{dt}</math>

and

:<math>ds^2 = g_{ij}(q) dq^i dq^j\,</math>

is the [[metric tensor]] on the manifold. Because this is the free-particle Hamiltonian, the solution to the [[Hamilton–Jacobi equation|Hamilton–Jacobi equations of motion]] are simply given by the [[geodesic]]s on the manifold.

Hadamard was able to show that all geodesics are unstable. All geodesics diverge exponentially from one another, as <math>e^{\lambda t}</math> with positive [[Lyapunov exponent]]
<!-- add proper modern proof with lyapunov -->
:<math>\lambda = \sqrt{\frac{2E}{mR^2}}</math>

with ''E'' the energy of a trajectory, and <math>K=-1/R^2</math> being the constant negative curvature of the surface.

== Surfaces with negative curvature ==
The [[Bolza surface]], can be such an example of constant negative curvature, i.e., a two-dimensional surface of genus two (a donut with two holes) and constant negative [[curvature]]; this is a compact [[Riemann surface]].
